cases.title: Newborn Respiratory Distress
cases.stem: A term male newborn is delivered after a prolonged labour. Five minutes after birth, the nurse notes persistent grunting, nasal flaring, intercostal retractions, and central cyanosis despite routine drying and stimulation. The infant’s breathing appears laboured. The mother asks whether this is normal. The nurse knows that while some transitional findings can be expected, this pattern indicates probable respiratory distress requiring immediate action. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Newborn Respiratory Distress | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings are concerning for significant newborn respiratory distress? Select all that apply.

options.text: Retractions
Nasal flaring
Grunting
Laboured breathing
Central cyanosis

questions.rationale: All of these signs indicate increased work of breathing and poor oxygenation. Unlike benign transitional findings such as acrocyanosis, central cyanosis and significant respiratory effort are urgent. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Newborn Respiratory Distress | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Newborn respiratory distress requiring immediate assessment and support
Simple hunger cues
Normal newborn transition only
Mild sleepiness

questions.rationale: This infant is not transitioning normally. The pattern strongly indicates respiratory compromise. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Newborn Respiratory Distress | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Disturbed parent-infant bonding only
Impaired oxygenation and ineffective breathing in the newborn
Need for routine feeding
Bathing delay

questions.rationale: Airway and breathing always come first, especially in the newborn, who can deteriorate rapidly. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Newborn Respiratory Distress | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Initiate immediate newborn respiratory assessment and support according to neonatal protocol, and escalate urgently
Swaddle tightly and wait an hour
Feed the infant first
Assume cyanosis will resolve without reassessment

questions.rationale: The nurse must act immediately because this infant shows clear signs of respiratory distress. Delay may lead to severe hypoxia. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Newborn Respiratory Distress | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Observe for worsening grunting or apnea
Ignore retractions if the infant is term
Maintain thermoregulation while respiratory support is organised
Reassess colour, respiratory effort, and oxygenation frequently
Communicate clearly with the parent while continuing urgent care

questions.rationale: Respiratory distress management includes warmth, reassessment, communication, and observation for worsening fatigue or apnea. Term status does not make retractions normal. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Newborn Respiratory Distress | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Monitoring stops once the infant is quieter
Cyanosis persists and respirations become weaker
Colour improves, grunting decreases, breathing becomes easier, and the infant maintains better oxygenation
The infant becomes more lethargic without escalation

questions.rationale: Improved work of breathing and oxygenation indicate effective early management.

cases.title: Newborn Hypoglycaemia
cases.stem: A late preterm infant born to a mother with gestational diabetes is being monitored in the postnatal unit. A few hours after birth, the infant becomes jittery, sleepy, and demonstrates poor feeding. The nurse checks the glucose result and finds it below the expected safe range for the newborn. The infant is otherwise warm and pink but less vigorous than earlier. The nurse recognises newborn hypoglycaemia as a priority problem because the brain is highly sensitive to low glucose. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Newborn Hypoglycaemia | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings support neonatal hypoglycaemia? Select all that apply.

options.text: Poor feeding
Sleepiness/lethargy
Low glucose reading
Jitteriness
Infant of a mother with gestational diabetes

questions.rationale: All of these factors support neonatal hypoglycaemia. Infants of diabetic mothers are at particular risk because of altered glucose-insulin adaptation after birth. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Newborn Hypoglycaemia | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Benign sleep cycle
Mild cold stress alone
Neonatal hypoglycaemia requiring prompt treatment and reassessment
Normal newborn behaviour only

questions.rationale: Low glucose with symptoms must be treated promptly. Waiting risks worsening neurological compromise. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Newborn Hypoglycaemia | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Disturbed family sleep
Inadequate glucose availability to the newborn brain
Delayed bathing
Need for routine discharge teaching

questions.rationale: In neonatal hypoglycaemia, neurological protection is the main priority. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Newborn Hypoglycaemia | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Bathe the infant before feeding
Delay action until the next routine blood sugar check
Ignore symptoms if the infant is warm
Initiate feeding or other protocol-based glucose support promptly and reassess the infant closely

questions.rationale: Rapid correction and close reassessment are required. Hypoglycaemia should not be left untreated simply because the infant looks otherwise stable. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Newborn Hypoglycaemia | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Recheck glucose after treatment according to protocol
Assume one low reading is never important
Explain the situation calmly to the parents
Maintain warmth and reduce energy expenditure
Monitor feeding effectiveness and tone

questions.rationale: Thermoregulation, repeat glucose testing, feeding assessment, and parent communication are all appropriate. A low symptomatic reading is always important. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Newborn Hypoglycaemia | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: The infant becomes weaker without escalation
Lethargy worsens and feeding remains poor
Monitoring stops after one feed
Glucose rises to a safer range, feeding improves, jitteriness resolves, and the infant becomes more alert

questions.rationale: Improvement is reflected in both biochemical correction and clinical behaviour.

cases.title: Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia
cases.stem: A 3-day-old newborn is brought to the nursery for assessment because the mother notices increasing yellow discoloration of the skin and eyes. The infant is feeding but appears sleepier than on the previous day. The bilirubin result is above the safe threshold for the infant’s age and clinical context. The nurse must assess severity, feeding adequacy, and risk of worsening jaundice while preparing for phototherapy and parent teaching if ordered. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings support clinically important neonatal jaundice? Select all that apply.

options.text: Need to assess feeding pattern
Increased sleepiness
Yellow discoloration of skin and sclera
Elevated bilirubin level
Newborn age of 3 days

questions.rationale: All the listed points matter. Jaundice is common in newborns, but rising bilirubin plus sleepiness and feeding concerns can indicate a need for treatment and close monitoring. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The infant has postpartum depression
The infant may have clinically significant hyperbilirubinemia requiring monitoring and possibly phototherapy
The colour change is unrelated to bilirubin
This can never be significant because jaundice is always normal

questions.rationale: Physiologic jaundice may be common, but significant bilirubin elevation can be harmful. The nurse must assess severity and follow treatment thresholds. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Umbilical cord stump education only
Risk for bilirubin-related neurological injury if levels rise further
Need for routine bathing advice
Disturbed sleep pattern of the parents

questions.rationale: Very high bilirubin can become dangerous, so preventing neurological injury is the priority. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop feeding the infant
Assess feeding and elimination, verify bilirubin trends, and prepare for phototherapy or other management as ordered
Ignore sleepiness if the infant is yellow
Delay all care until the next day

questions.rationale: Feeding and bilirubin trend assessment are crucial because poor intake can worsen jaundice. Delaying care or stopping feeds would be unsafe. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assume jaundice will always resolve without follow-up
Observe for worsening lethargy or poor feeding
Reassess bilirubin according to protocol
Monitor hydration and feeding effectiveness
Provide parent education about jaundice and phototherapy if used

questions.rationale: Safe newborn care includes monitoring, education, and follow-up. A passive wait-and-see approach is inappropriate when bilirubin is already elevated. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Bilirubin trends down, feeding improves, and the infant is more alert
Sleepiness increases and feeding declines
Phototherapy is started but never reassessed
Parents remain uninformed about warning signs

questions.rationale: Improvement is shown by falling bilirubin and better feeding/alertness.

cases.title: Neonatal Sepsis
cases.stem: A newborn delivered after prolonged rupture of membranes becomes increasingly lethargic within the first day of life. The infant feeds poorly, has temperature instability, and shows periods of mottled skin and intermittent grunting. The mother asks why the baby seems less responsive than immediately after birth. The nurse understands that newborn sepsis may present subtly and can deteriorate rapidly. The infant requires urgent assessment and escalation. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Neonatal Sepsis | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings raise concern for neonatal sepsis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Mottling and grunting
Poor feeding
Lethargy
Prolonged rupture of membranes
Temperature instability

questions.rationale: All these findings are concerning. Neonatal sepsis often presents with non-specific signs, so nurses must respond quickly to subtle deterioration. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Neonatal Sepsis | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Mild jaundice only
Possible neonatal sepsis requiring urgent evaluation and treatment
Benign adaptation
Normal newborn tiredness

questions.rationale: The symptom cluster plus prolonged rupture of membranes makes infection a serious concern. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Neonatal Sepsis | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Parent inconvenience
Risk for overwhelming infection and respiratory compromise in the newborn
Need for discharge teaching
Delayed infant bath

questions.rationale: Newborn sepsis can become life-threatening quickly. The priority is survival and prevention of rapid decline. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Neonatal Sepsis | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Escalate urgently, support thermoregulation and respiratory assessment, and prepare for sepsis evaluation and treatment as ordered
Wait to see whether the infant perks up after sleep
Feed only when convenient later
Stop monitoring because the baby is quiet

questions.rationale: Urgent action is required because newborn sepsis may progress rapidly. Thermoregulation and respiratory support are important immediate priorities. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Neonatal Sepsis | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Support family understanding while urgent care continues
Ignore grunting if the infant is term
Anticipate cultures and antibiotic therapy as ordered
Monitor colour, tone, respirations, and feeding closely
Reassess temperature and perfusion frequently

questions.rationale: Close observation and family communication are important. Grunting is a serious respiratory sign and must not be ignored. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Neonatal Sepsis | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Lethargy deepens and grunting worsens
Perfusion is not reassessed
Feeding improves, colour and tone stabilise, temperature becomes more consistent, and respiratory effort eases
Monitoring stops after antibiotics start

questions.rationale: Improvement must be seen in behaviour, temperature, perfusion, and breathing.

cases.title: Preterm Infant with Respiratory Distress Syndrome
cases.stem: A 32-week preterm infant is admitted to the neonatal care area shortly after birth. The nurse observes tachypnoea, grunting, nasal flaring, and subcostal retractions. The infant is small, has minimal respiratory reserve, and requires support to maintain temperature and oxygenation. The mother is anxious and asks whether the baby will be able to breathe independently. The nurse recognises the pattern as consistent with respiratory distress syndrome related to prematurity. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Preterm Infant with Respiratory Distress Syndrome | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings support respiratory distress syndrome in a preterm infant? Select all that apply.

options.text: Grunting and nasal flaring
Retractions
Reduced physiological reserve
Tachypnoea
Prematurity at 32 weeks

questions.rationale: Prematurity strongly predisposes to surfactant deficiency and RDS. The visible work of breathing confirms respiratory compromise. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Preterm Infant with Respiratory Distress Syndrome | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Normal newborn transition only
Benign feeding difficulty
Respiratory distress syndrome requiring close support of breathing and thermoregulation
Stable sleep pattern

questions.rationale: The infant’s prematurity and clear respiratory distress signs indicate RDS rather than normal transition. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Preterm Infant with Respiratory Distress Syndrome | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Delayed naming ceremony
Need for routine cord teaching only
Impaired gas exchange and risk of worsening fatigue in the premature infant
Parent fatigue

questions.rationale: Airway and breathing are always first, especially in preterm infants who fatigue quickly. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Preterm Infant with Respiratory Distress Syndrome | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Ignore the grunting because preterm infants are noisy
Delay intervention to allow longer skin-to-skin time only
Bathe the infant immediately
Support airway and breathing according to neonatal protocol, maintain thermoregulation, and escalate for advanced neonatal management

questions.rationale: The infant requires respiratory and thermal support immediately. Delay may worsen hypoxia and exhaustion. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Preterm Infant with Respiratory Distress Syndrome | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Support parent understanding while urgent care continues
Prepare for neonatal respiratory support measures as ordered
Minimise energy expenditure and unnecessary stimulation
Assume the infant will self-correct without reassessment
Reassess colour, work of breathing, and oxygenation frequently

questions.rationale: A preterm infant with RDS needs close reassessment, energy conservation, and timely escalation. Parent communication remains important. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Preterm Infant with Respiratory Distress Syndrome | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Temperature falls further without action
Retractions worsen and the infant becomes more lethargic
Monitoring stops once the infant is quieter
Respiratory effort lessens, oxygenation improves, and the infant maintains temperature and colour more effectively

questions.rationale: Improvement is shown by easier breathing, better oxygenation, and more stable thermal control.
